title: Advertising Techniques: 15 Types with Examples
summary: 15 advertising techniques with real examples: testimonial, scarcity, demonstration, bandwagon and more, plus a goal table and how to test which wins.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- **Advertising techniques** are the persuasion methods inside an ad, such as testimonial, scarcity, demonstration, storytelling and humor.
- Fifteen common ones: testimonial, celebrity, expert, bandwagon, scarcity, demonstration, problem and solution, comparison, storytelling, humor, repetition, snob appeal, plain folks, transfer and price anchoring.
- Pick one lead technique per ad and one or two supports.
- Test techniques head to head with the same offer and audience.


## What advertising techniques are


Advertising techniques are the repeatable methods ads use to get attention and move a viewer toward a decision. A technique is not a channel or a format. It is the persuasion move inside the ad: a celebrity, a demonstration, a countdown, a story. One ad often uses two or three at once.


Below are 15 techniques with a real or typical example of each, a note on when it works, and a table to pick from. If you want the channel view instead, see[types of advertising](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/types-of-advertising) . For the feeling-led techniques, see[emotional appeal in advertising](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/emotional-appeal-in-advertising) .


## 15 advertising techniques with examples


### 1. Testimonial


A real customer says the product worked. Weight loss and software ads lean on it. It works best when the person looks like the buyer and the result is specific: "I cut my invoicing time from four hours to forty minutes."


### 2. Celebrity endorsement


A famous face lends attention and status. Nike and Michael Jordan is the textbook case. The risk is cost and the chance the person later becomes a liability.


### 3. Expert or authority


A dentist, chef or engineer vouches. Toothpaste ads that show a dentist in a white coat use it. It lifts credibility for products where the buyer cannot judge quality.


### 4. Bandwagon and social proof


"Join 40,000 teams." The ad says many people already chose this, so it must be safe. Ratings, review counts and customer logos all use it.


### 5. Scarcity and urgency


Limited stock, limited time, a countdown. It speeds up a decision a buyer already leans toward. It backfires if the scarcity is fake.


### 6. Demonstration


Show the product doing the job. Blendtec's "Will It Blend?" videos put a blender through an iPhone and made the product the entertainment. Demonstration is the best answer to "does it really work?"


### 7. Problem and solution


Open on a pain, then offer the fix. "Spent your Sunday on spreadsheets?" works because the viewer recognises themselves in the first line.


### 8. Comparison


Set your product against a rival or a past habit. Apple's Mac vs PC ads did this with two actors. Comparisons must be fair and provable, or they become the misleading ads we cover in[misleading advertising examples](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/misleading-advertising-examples) .


### 9. Storytelling


A small narrative with a beginning, a turn and a payoff. Airbnb and Dove tell stories about people, not rooms or soap. Stories are remembered longer than claims.


### 10. Humor


A laugh buys attention and goodwill. Old Spice reinvented its image with an absurd monologue. Humor is risky when the joke overshadows the product.


### 11. Repetition and slogans


Say the same line enough that it sticks. "Just Do It", "I'm lovin' it" and "Think different" work through years of repetition. Retargeting is the paid-social version.


### 12. Snob appeal


Position the product as for the discerning few. Luxury watches and premium spirits use it. The ad sells status, not specs.


### 13. Plain folks


The opposite: ordinary people, ordinary setting, honest voice. User-generated style ads use it. See the[UGC ads guide](https://www.sprites.ai/guides/what-are-ugc-ads) .


### 14. Transfer


Link the product to something the audience already loves: a place, a song, a cause. A car shown on an empty coastal road is borrowing the feeling of freedom.


### 15. Price anchoring and offers


Show the higher price first, then the one you want them to pay, or bundle a bonus. "Was $120, now $79" frames the saving. The old price must have been a real price for the claim to be honest.


## Which technique for which goal


Goal Techniques that fit Where it shows up


Get attention Humor, storytelling, celebrity, surprise Video, social feeds, TV


Build trust Testimonial, expert, demonstration Landing pages, search ads


Drive a decision now Scarcity, offers, social proof Retargeting, email, shopping ads


Stand out from rivals Comparison, snob appeal, plain folks Paid social, display


Be remembered Repetition, slogans, storytelling Brand campaigns


## How techniques stack in one ad


Take a meal kit ad for a Meta feed. Open with problem and solution ("It is 6pm and nobody has a plan"), show a short demonstration (box open, pan on the stove), add a testimonial overlay from a parent, and close with an offer and a soft deadline. That is four techniques in 20 seconds.


Good stacking has one lead technique and one or two supports. Five techniques in one frame is noise. Pick the lead from the table above, then support it.


## Writing it: three worked examples


Technique Weak line Stronger line


Problem and solution Our scheduling tool saves time. Stop answering "when are you free?" six times a week.


Social proof Many customers love us. 4,200 clinics book through one link.


Demonstration See how it works. Watch a 3-minute install, start to first sale.


The stronger lines are specific and checkable. The numbers above are illustrations of the style, not claims about any real product. Replace them with your own proven figures. More formats to borrow are in[ad copy examples](https://www.sprites.ai/ad-copy-examples) , and openers are covered in[ad hook styles](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/ad-hook-styles) .


## How to test which technique wins


1. Fix the offer, audience and budget. Change only the technique.
2. Run three variants, for example testimonial, demonstration and scarcity.
3. Let each get enough impressions to separate. A few hundred clicks each is a minimum for conversion rate reads.
4. Keep the winner, then test a second technique on top of it.
5. Re-test every few months. Techniques wear out as audiences see them.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are advertising techniques?


Advertising techniques are the persuasion methods inside an ad, such as testimonials, celebrity endorsement, scarcity, demonstration and storytelling. They describe how the ad persuades, not where it runs.


### What are examples of advertising techniques?


Common ones are testimonial, celebrity endorsement, expert authority, bandwagon, scarcity, demonstration, problem and solution, comparison, storytelling, humor, repetition, snob appeal, plain folks, transfer and price anchoring.


### What is the most effective advertising technique?


There is no single winner. Demonstration and testimonials tend to build trust, and scarcity speeds up decisions that are already leaning your way. The best choice depends on the product and what the buyer doubts. Test two or three against each other.


### What is the difference between advertising techniques and advertising types?


Types describe the channel or format, such as print, TV, digital or outdoor. Techniques describe the persuasion move inside the ad. A single TV ad and a single social ad can use the same technique.


### What is the bandwagon technique in advertising?


The bandwagon technique says many people already use a product, so you should too. Review counts, "join 40,000 customers" and customer logo bars are all bandwagon appeals.


### Can I use more than one technique in an ad?


Yes, and most ads do. Choose one lead technique and one or two supports. Stacking too many in a single ad dilutes the message.
